intro: Cache keys need consistent representation when dictionary insertion order differs. Sorting object keys and fixing separators removes those incidental formatting differences.
task: Produce deterministic compact JSON with sorted object keys and finite numbers only.
requirements: Accept bounded plain data, but sequences must be lists and object keys must be nonempty strings. Return compact json.dumps output with sorted keys, ensure_ascii=False, allow_nan=False, and separators comma/colon without spaces. Preserve Python JSON distinctions such as 1 versus 1.0; this is not a cross-language canonical-JSON standard.

Sequence inputs are Python lists or tuples of at most 1000 items. Text inputs contain valid Unicode scalar characters and at most 10000 characters. Identifier and dictionary keys are nonempty strings of at most 100 characters. Numeric values are finite Python ints or floats with magnitude at most 1e9; bool is not numeric. Plain record data may contain strings, numbers, booleans, None, lists, tuples, and dictionaries; nesting is limited to six levels and dictionaries to 1000 keys.
Return the documented Python output types and preserve all caller inputs. Raise ValueError for invalid inputs unless the task explicitly reports a record-level rejection.

hints.title: Trace one record
hints.body: Sort keys recursively through the serializer, but never sort array items.

hints.title: Handle the boundary
hints.body: Use a strict finite-data check before serialization; otherwise NaN may become nonstandard JSON.

explanation: Cache keys need consistent representation when dictionary insertion order differs. Sorting object keys and fixing separators removes those incidental formatting differences.
Arrays keep their order because order is part of their meaning. This deterministic Python encoding is useful within a controlled pipeline without claiming every runtime encodes numbers identically.
